title: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
hook: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
tomorrow: the word Pope Francis kept saying

segments.voice: Yesterday: Easter, the women, and the stone already moved. Today, one of the saints from day five, up close. Day seventeen.

Italy, the Middle Ages. A town on a hill called Assisi. There's a young man there everyone knows: the son of a rich cloth merchant, good clothes, good parties, the one who pays for everybody's dinner. He dreams of being a knight. He goes off to a war with the next town, gets captured, spends a long stretch in a prison cell, and comes home sick. And something in him has changed. He starts giving things away. Money, cloth from his father's shop. His father is furious, and drags him in front of the bishop of Assisi, in the town square, to get his property back. What the son does next is why people still know his name.
screen: `ASSISI, A TOWN ON A HILL.` → `THE RICH MERCHANT'S SON.` → `DRAGGED BEFORE THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: His name was Francesco. We say Francis. According to the stories written down by his early followers, he stood in front of the bishop and the whole town, took off his clothes, every piece, and handed them back to his father. And he said, in effect: until now I called you my father. From now on I'll say our Father, who art in heaven. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis walked out of town with nothing. What came next is the part people forget. He didn't become a hermit. He went toward the people everyone avoided. The stories say that once, riding outside town, he met a man with leprosy, a disease that made people outcasts, and instead of riding past, he got down and kissed his hand. Later he wrote that what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness. He gathered friends who lived poor, preached in the streets and cared for the sick. They became the Franciscans, who still carry his name. Near the end of his life he wrote a song, the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for brother sun and sister moon, even sister death. Now today's line: lord, make me an instrument. It opens the prayer that bears his name, make me an instrument of your peace. Here's the honest part. As far as anyone can tell, Francis didn't write it. Its first known printing is in a small French magazine in 1912, with no author's name. His name was attached to it later. Francis's own words are in the Canticle.
screen: `HE GAVE THE CLOTHES BACK.` · `TOWARD THE PEOPLE EVERYONE AVOIDED.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` · `THE PRAYER HE PROBABLY DIDN'T WRITE.` · then, large: `MAKE ME AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Get comfortable and let your breath slow down. Think of one thing you're holding on to a little too tightly. It doesn't have to be big. A grudge counts. With each breath out, imagine loosening your grip on it, the way Francis handed his clothes back. If you pray, you can say the line: lord, make me an instrument.
Francis. Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back and went toward the outcasts. Seventeenth word.
Your line: lord, make me an instrument. The prayer borrowed his name; the life was his own. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WORD POPE FRANCIS KEPT SAYING.`

howItsDone: Catholics keep a feast day for Saint Francis each year, and some parishes bless pets and animals around it; the Peace Prayer, first printed in 1912, is often prayed in his name.

fork.setup: your furious father has dragged you before the bishop in the town square to get his property back. you're Francis. what do you do?
options: apologize and go back to the shop.
take off your clothes and hand them back.
fork.reveal: he gave back everything, down to his clothes, and said he'd now call only God our Father. the bishop covered him with his cloak.

original.note: Umbrian Italian, not Latin: praised be you, my Lord. the refrain of Francis's Canticle of the Creatures.

trapdoor: what you thought: the saint with the birds on the garden statue.
what it means: a rich merchant's son who gave everything back and went toward the outcasts.
what a scholar hears: the Canticle, written in his own Umbrian dialect rather than Latin; the Peace Prayer, anonymous, first printed in La Clochette in 1912.
